newsitem.title: USA: Key U.S. congressman blasts bank reform proposal.
newsitem.headline: Key U.S. congressman blasts bank reform proposal.

text.p: The chairman of a House subcommittee reworking U.S. financial modernization legislation on Wednesday strongly criticized the bill as reported out of the Banking Committee.

Rep. Michael Oxley, head of the Commerce Committee's finance subcommittee, said the bill to overhaul the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act and other financial laws would create an uneven playing field without streamlining current regulations.

"These hearings have underscored the importance of two recurring themes -- fair competition and efficient regulation," the Ohio Republican said at a hearing on Wednesday. "The approach taken in (the bill) as it currently stands does not achieve either of these goals."
"It doesn't even come close," he added.

If enacted, the bill would allow banks, securities firms and insurance companies to enter one another's businesses. Commercial companies, such as automakers and health-care providers, would also be permitted to own banks.
Oxley outlined four specific parts of the legislation that he said needed to be reworked. The subcommittee plans to amend and vote on the bill shortly after the August recess.

The bill would continue to allow banks to conduct some securities activities without oversight from the Securities and Exchange Commission. Oxley said such a system "ensures only continued confusion of investors, uneven protection of investors, and competitive disparities between banks and securities firms."
The bill would also allow the Federal Reserve to have some oversight of holding companies that owned banks but also had other significant affiliates that were not banks.
Oxley said he was "pleased" by earlier testimony of Fed chairman Alan Greenspan that the central bank should not supervise holding companies that are not primarily engaged in banking.
"Safety and soundness regulation of securities firms, mutual funds and insurance companies is neither safe nor sound for our capital markets," he said.
Oxley said a new council of state and federal regulators created by the bill "would create many more problems that it was designed to resolve."
The subcommittee chairman also spoke out against allowing banks to engage in non-banking activities through direct subsidiaries rather than through affiliates owned by the same holding company.
"We need a framework that does not put taxpayers in the position of subsidizing the securities activities of bank subsidiaries," Oxley said.

Oxley did state his intention to retain provisions of the bill allowing some mixing of banking and commerce. "Failing to provide for some relief on this front would deny the benefits of a modern regulatory structure to many existing financial service providers," he said.
The Commerce Committee has until mid-September to complete its work on the bank reform bill, which was passed narrowly by the Banking Committee last month.

Even if the committee approves a bill, the legislation faces an uncertain fate. Congress has been trying for more than a decade without success to reform Glass-Steagall and overhaul financial regulations.
